summary: Describes Cisco's Layer Two Forwarding protocol, which tunnels the link layer of higher-level protocols, such as HDLC, async HDLC or SLIP frames. It is a historic protocol and was a forerunner of later tunneling standards.

plainLanguage.summary: L2F lets a person dial in to their internet provider as usual and still land inside their own network. The provider's dial-up server opens a tunnel to a gateway at the user's site and passes the raw link-layer frames through it, so the user's own equipment sees an ordinary dial-up connection.

what is a home gateway in l2f
subtitle: A tunneling protocol that carries a dial-up user's link-layer frames to their own home network.

tldr.problem: A remote user who dials in to an internet service provider usually gets an address from that provider and reaches only the provider's network, not the private network at home or at work.
tldr.mechanism: L2F carries the user's link-layer frames, PPP or SLIP, inside a tunnel from the provider's dial-up server to the home gateway, so the home site sees an ordinary dial-in connection and assigns the address itself.
tldr.outcome: The RFC defines the packet format, the management messages, the tunnel and client setup sequences and the accounting rules. It is a Historic protocol and the RFC itself says it specifies no Internet standard.

facts.label: Checksum
facts.value: 16-bit CRC as used by PPP and HDLC (FCS-16)

today: RFC 2341 is Historic: the RFC itself describes the protocol as historic and says it specifies no Internet standard, and the unit metadata lists no replacement RFC for it. It was published in May 1998 and remains an experimental document, with parts of its scope, such as operation under Apple's ARAP protocol, left without an implementation.

sections.title: Why Virtual Dial-Up Needs a Tunnel
sections.content:
The traditional dial-up service on the Internet is for registered IP addresses only. The RFC describes a different class of service, virtual dial-up, which allows multiple protocols and unregistered IP addresses, for example privately addressed IP, IPX and AppleTalk dial-up carried over SLIP or PPP across existing Internet infrastructure. The benefit is that a very large investment in access and core infrastructure can be shared, local calls can be used, and existing non-IP applications can be supported securely while still riding on the Internet's access infrastructure.

The user of such a service is assumed to want everything a dedicated dial-up line gives. The remote end system and the home site hosts must need no special software. Authentication must be available as PPP CHAP or PAP, or through other dialogs for protocols such as SLIP, including TACACS+ and RADIUS solutions and support for smart cards and one-time passwords, and the user must be able to manage it independently of the provider. Addressing must be as manageable as with a dedicated line, with the address assigned by the home site rather than the provider. Authorization must be managed by the home site, and accounting must be possible both for the provider's billing and for the user's own charge-back and auditing.

The topology the RFC assumes has a home gateway at the user's site, home LANs behind it, routers on the Internet, remote users dialling in over the PSTN or ISDN, and the provider's network access server at the point of presence. A remote user reaches the home LAN as if they had dialled into the home gateway directly, even though the physical connection goes through the provider's network access server.
sections.plainLanguage: Dial in to a provider and you normally get one of their addresses and reach their network, not yours. L2F is for the case where the user wants to reach their own network instead, with their own addresses and their own rules, while the telephone call still goes to the provider.

sections.title: How a Virtual Dial-Up Session Works
sections.content:
The RFC walks through a complete session. The remote user starts a PPP connection to the provider over the PSTN or ISDN. The network access server accepts it and the PPP link is established. The provider then does a partial authentication with CHAP or PAP, and interprets only the username field to decide whether the user wants a virtual dial-up service. Usernames are expected, though not required, to be structured, such as littlewo@cisco.com; alternatively the provider may keep a database mapping users to services, and for a virtual dial-up user that mapping names a specific endpoint, the home gateway.

If no tunnel to the wanted home gateway exists yet, one is created. L2F is deliberately insulated from the details of the media carrying the tunnel, and requires only that the media provide packet-oriented point-to-point connectivity. The RFC names UDP, Frame Relay permanent virtual circuits and X.25 virtual circuits as examples. Once the tunnel exists, an unused multiplex ID is allocated and a connect indication is sent to the home gateway to announce the new session. The home gateway either accepts or rejects, and a rejection may carry a reason that is shown to the user before the call is disconnected.

The connect indication can carry the authentication information the provider gathered, so that the home gateway can complete the authentication itself without another round. For CHAP that means the challenge, the user name and the raw response; for PAP or a plain text dialog it means the user name and the clear-text password. For PPP it can also carry copies of the LCP CONFACK packets sent in each direction to complete LCP negotiation, which lets the home gateway initialise its own PPP state or start a fresh LCP CONFREQ exchange.

When the home gateway accepts, it creates a virtual interface for SLIP or PPP, much as it would for a directly dialled connection, and link-layer frames can now pass over the tunnel in both directions. Frames from the remote user arrive at the provider's point of presence, are stripped of their link framing and transparency bytes, are encapsulated in L2F and are forwarded over the tunnel. The home gateway strips the L2F header and processes them as ordinary incoming frames. The virtual interface behaves much like a hardware interface, except that the hardware sits at the provider's point of presence rather than at the user's site. Accounting can be done at both ends.
sections.plainLanguage: The provider checks the user name to find out which home network the call belongs to, opens a tunnel to that network, and passes the connection along with the credentials it already collected. From then on the call behaves like an ordinary dial-in to the home site.

sections.title: Authentication, Addresses and Accounting
sections.content:
On security, the provider authenticates only far enough to discover the user's apparent identity and, by implication, the home gateway they want. It then opens a connection to that gateway carrying the information it gathered, and the home gateway completes the authentication by accepting or rejecting. The home gateway must also protect itself against third parties opening tunnels to it, so tunnel establishment includes an authentication phase between the provider and the home gateway.

On addressing, the ordinary Internet service hands out addresses from a pool of provider addresses, which often means the remote user has little or no access to the home network's resources because firewalls apply to traffic from outside addresses. With virtual dial-up the home gateway can sit behind the home firewall and allocate internal addresses, which may be private addresses under RFC 1597 or addresses of another kind entirely. Because L2F tunnels exclusively at the frame layer, the address management policy is irrelevant to the correctness of the service: for all purposes of PPP or SLIP handling, the dial-in user appears to have connected at the home gateway.

Authentication happens in three phases. The first is at the provider, which uses the user name to decide a virtual dial-up service is needed and to open the tunnel. The second is at the home gateway, which decides whether to accept the connection using the CHAP, PAP or textual information it was sent. The third is optional, at the PPP or SLIP layer, and lies outside the scope of the specification, but might include another cycle of LCP authentication, proprietary PPP extensions or textual challenges carried over a TCP/IP telnet session.

For accounting, the RFC makes it a requirement that both the access gateway and the home gateway can produce accounting data, so both may count packets, octets and connection start and stop times. Because the home gateway can decline a connection on the strength of the information the provider collected, the accounting can tell a series of failed connection attempts apart from a series of brief successful connections. Without that facility the home gateway would have to accept every request and exchange PPP packets with the remote system to find out.
sections.plainLanguage: Four things have to be worked out: who is calling, which address they get, who decides what they may do, and how the call is billed. L2F splits these between the provider and the home site, with the home site making the final decision on all of them.

sections.title: The L2F Packet Header
sections.content:
An L2F packet is an L2F header, the payload packet, which is the SLIP or PPP frame, and an optional L2F checksum. When PPP is carried, the encapsulated packet is the packet as it would be transmitted over a physical link, with the flags, the transparency data and the CRC removed but the address and control flags and the protocol value still present. SLIP is encapsulated in much the same way, with the transparency characters and the framing removed first.

The header carries a set of flag bits and then the fields. The F bit says that a payload offset is present. The K bit says a packet key is present. The P bit marks a priority packet, and the RFC recommends that PPP keepalive traffic be sent with it set. The S bit says a sequence number is present and must be set for all L2F management packets. Eight bits after the S bit are reserved and must be zero. The C bit says a checksum follows the payload.

The three-bit Version field holds the major version of the L2F software and must contain the value 001. A packet whose version is not 1, or that has non-zero bits between the S bit and the C bit, carries extensions the receiver does not understand and is handled as an invalid packet. The 16-bit Protocol field says what the packet carries: 0x00 is illegal, 0x01 is an L2F management packet, 0x02 is PPP tunnelled inside L2F and 0x03 is SLIP tunnelled inside L2F.

The 16-bit Sequence field is present when the S bit is set. It starts at 0 for the first sequenced packet of each multiplex ID and is a free running counter modulo 256. The receiver records the sequence number of each valid packet and silently discards any packet whose value is less than or equal to the last one it accepted, which is how duplicates are caught. A value counts as less than or equal when it falls in the range of the last value and its 127 successor values, so with 15 as the last value, numbers 0 through 15 and 144 through 255 are discarded.

The 16-bit Multiplex ID identifies one connection within the tunnel, and each new connection gets a value not currently in use. The RFC recommends that the value cycle through the whole 16-bit space to reduce aliasing between sessions. The value 0 is special and carries the state of the tunnel itself, so only L2F management packets may use it. The 16-bit Client ID helps the endpoints sort out which packets belong to which tunnel when several tunnels arrive interleaved over the same point-to-point media. The value the peer assigned during L2F_CONF is used on every later packet sent to it, packets with an unknown client ID are silently discarded, and the first packet of a tunnel carries 0.

The 16-bit Length is the size in octets of the whole packet, header and payload, not counting the checksum. A shorter packet is discarded and extra bytes beyond the stated length are ignored. The optional 16-bit Offset, present when the F bit is set, says how many bytes past the header the payload begins. The optional 32-bit Key, present when the K bit is set, is derived from the authentication response given when the tunnel was created, and resists spoofing for the life of the session; a packet whose key does not match is silently discarded. The optional checksum is the 16-bit CRC used by PPP and HDLC, applied from the first byte of the L2F flags to the last byte of the payload and appended after the payload.
sections.plainLanguage: Each L2F packet has a fixed header describing what it carries, which connection it belongs to and how to check it. Most of the header fields are fixed size, and a few are only present when a flag bit says so, which keeps the overhead small.

sections.title: Establishing a Tunnel and a Client
sections.content:
When the point-to-point link between the network access server and the home gateway is first brought up, the two ends talk on multiplex ID 0 before serving any clients. This exchange verifies that L2F is present at the far end and allows any authentication that is needed. The protocol value is 1, meaning L2F management, and the body of the message is a sequence of single octets naming an option, followed by octets formatted as that option requires.

The tunnel negotiation has four steps. The network access server sends an L2F_CONF with the sequence number 0, multiplex ID 0, client ID 0 and a key of 0, and the body carries its claimed name, a challenge random number and the client ID value it has chosen for the peer. The home gateway replies with its own L2F_CONF, giving its name, its own challenge and its own assigned client ID. The access server then sends an L2F_OPEN whose response is the hash of the challenge it received, and sets the packet key from the shared secret; the home gateway answers with the matching hash, which closes the key exchange. From that point every packet carries the key, and the tunnel is ready for clients.

Establishing a client on that tunnel takes four more steps. The access server allocates the next free multiplex ID and sends an L2F_OPEN carrying the authentication type, the user name, and for CHAP the challenge, the response and the identifier. The home gateway answers with an L2F_OPEN of its own, which accepts the client. After that, PPP frames flow in both directions inside L2F, carrying the same sequence number of 0 because the data traffic is not L2F control traffic.

The management messages themselves are built from options. An option is a single octet naming a message type, followed by sub-options. The message types are L2F_CONF to request configuration, L2F_OPEN to accept configuration and to open a client, L2F_CLOSE to disconnect, and L2F_ECHO and L2F_ECHO_RESP to check that the peer is still there. A packet with an invalid message type, or with an illegal field, must be discarded and an L2F_CLOSE of the whole tunnel requested, although a packet with a wrong key is discarded without disconnecting, which stops denial-of-service attempts. L2F_CLOSE carries a bit mask of reasons, such as authentication failed, out of resources, administrative intervention, user quota exceeded, protocol error or unknown user, and may carry an ASCII description. L2F_ECHO is optional, no implementation may send more than one per second, and its payload must be 64 bytes or less.

L2F is designed to run over point-to-point unreliable links. It does not provide flow control or reliable delivery for the data traffic; each protocol tunnel carried inside L2F is expected to manage flow control and retries itself. Only the L2F control messages have to be retransmitted, and they all carry a sequence number so the receiver can spot duplicates.
sections.plainLanguage: Setting up takes two rounds. First the provider and the home site agree a secret and label each other's packets, so neither end can be impersonated. Then, for each call, the provider passes the user's credentials across and the home site accepts or rejects. Only the setup messages are reliable; the user's data is left to PPP to manage.

sections.title: Running L2F Over IP and UDP
sections.content:
Because L2F carries uninterpreted frames, it lets the two PPP endpoints negotiate higher-level features such as a reliable link, compression, multi-link and encryption without L2F needing to know about them. PPP echo requests, NCP configuration negotiation and even termination requests are simply tunnelled HDLC frames. L2F does not detect a frame such as a PPP TERMREQ: termination is driven from a protocol endpoint, so if the home gateway receives a TERMREQ it hangs up the PPP session, and the L2F implementation at the home gateway turns that hang-up into an L2F_CLOSE that shuts the client's session down cleanly, optionally with a reason code and a text description.

L2F works with both PAP and CHAP. SLIP offers no authentication of its own, so it requires an ASCII exchange of user name and password before SLIP starts, and L2F is compatible with that mode too. One-time password cards work to the extent that the access server can capture and forward the one-time password. The RFC also says that Apple's ARAP protocol appears compatible with L2F, but that its operation under L2F was not described because this experimental RFC has no corresponding implementation of it.

L2F runs over IP and UDP in a particular way. It uses the well-known UDP port 1701, and the entire L2F packet, header and payload alike, is sent inside one UDP datagram. The source and destination ports are the same, 1701, and tunnels are told apart by their client ID values rather than by port numbers. The source IP address for a given client ID may change over the life of a connection, which can happen when a peer with several interfaces answers after a topology change, and responses should reflect the last source address seen for that client ID. IP fragmentation may occur on the way, and L2F makes no special efforts to avoid it, though an access server may have its LCP negotiate a specific maximum receive unit to suit the path the L2F packets will take.
sections.plainLanguage: L2F can run over any point-to-point network, and the RFC works through how it behaves over the Internet. The whole packet travels inside one UDP datagram on port 1701, and several tunnels share that port, told apart by a tag in the header.

viz.caption: THE L2F HEADER AS DRAWN IN THE RFC

fields.name: F
fields.desc: Set when the payload offset field is present.

fields.name: K
fields.desc: Set when the packet key field is present.

fields.name: P
fields.desc: Set on a priority packet. PPP keepalive traffic should carry it.

fields.name: S
fields.desc: Set when the sequence number is present. It must be set for L2F management packets.

fields.name: Reserved
fields.desc: Must be zero in a version 1 packet. Any other value means the receiver does not understand the extensions.

fields.name: C
fields.desc: Set when a checksum follows the payload.

fields.name: Ver
fields.desc: Major version of the L2F software. It must contain the value 001.

fields.name: Protocol
fields.desc: What the packet carries: 0x00 illegal, 0x01 L2F management, 0x02 PPP tunnelled, 0x03 SLIP tunnelled.

fields.name: Sequence (opt)
fields.desc: Free running counter modulo 256, one per multiplex ID. Present only when the S bit is set.

fields.name: Multiplex ID
fields.desc: Identifies one connection within the tunnel. The value 0 carries the state of the tunnel itself.

fields.name: Client ID
fields.desc: Tag that identifies the peer and separates tunnels arriving interleaved over the same media.

fields.name: Length
fields.desc: Size in octets of the whole packet, header and payload, not counting the checksum.

fields.name: Offset (opt)
fields.desc: Number of bytes past the header at which the payload starts. Present only when the F bit is set.

fields.name: Key (opt)
fields.desc: Value derived from the authentication response, used to resist spoofing. Present only when the K bit is set.

items.label: L2F_ILLEGAL
items.desc: Illegal. A packet with this value must be treated as an illegal packet.

items.label: L2F_PROTO
items.desc: L2F management packets, the tunnel and client setup messages.
